content: The review found no data available for several outcomes, including child development, anemia, iron deficiency anemia, iron deficiency, hemoglobin levels, ferritin levels, nutrient intakes (sufficient or excessive), feeding practices, oral health, morbidity, dietary diversity, gut health, allergies, and outcomes related to phytoestrogens. For the comparison of animal milk (full-fat or lower-fat) versus plant-based milk, only one study (Svahn 1999) with 21 participants was included. This study was assessed as having a low risk of bias for confounding, attrition, and performance bias but a high risk of detection bias. The study reported no significant differences in serum lipid profiles, including low-density lipoproteins (LDL), high-density lipoproteins (HDL), and LDL/HDL ratios, between children aged 12–23 months consuming plant-based milk versus animal milk. The evidence was of low certainty. For the comparison of animal milk versus fortified milk, eight studies (2,905 participants) were included. Two studies (Sazawal 2007 and Stecksén-Blicks 2009) were assessed as having a lower risk of bias, while others were at higher risk. Sensitivity analyses retained the lower-risk studies and temporarily excluded higher-risk studies to assess their impact on the results. One study (Svahn 1999) reported on weight outcomes, showing low-certainty evidence. Another study (Sazawal 2007) reported on stunting and wasting, with low-certainty evidence. Fortified milk was associated with higher hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations compared to animal milk when consumed at 150 mL/day for at least four months. Fortified milk also reduced the risk of anemia and iron deficiency anemia compared to animal milk when consumed at 400 mL/day. Regarding nutrient status, two studies (Stekel 1988 and Svahn 1999) reported on serum iron concentrations, and two others (Sazawal 2007 and Villalpando 2006) reported on plasma zinc concentrations. Fortified milk was associated with higher serum zinc concentrations and a lower likelihood of anemia compared to animal milk. One study (Stecksén-Blicks 2009) reported on oral health, showing that children consuming fortified milk were more likely to be caries-free compared to those consuming animal milk. The review also included qualitative analyses of non-randomized studies. For example, Ghisolfi (2012) found that children consuming 250 mL of cow’s milk daily had a higher risk of insufficient intake of several nutrients, such as linoleic acid, alpha-linolenic acid, iron, vitamin C, and vitamin D, compared to those consuming follow-on formula. Follow-on formula reduced the risk of nutrient insufficiency, except for protein intake, which was higher in the cow’s milk group. The evidence on plant-based and lower-fat milks was limited. One study (Svahn 1999) reported no significant differences in lipid serum profiles between children consuming plant-based milk and those consuming animal milk. No data were available on the effects of animal milk versus no milk on child development, stool characteristics, or other outcomes. The quality of evidence was mixed, with many studies having methodological limitations, such as unclear randomization methods, lack of blinding, and small sample sizes. Sensitivity analyses showed that excluding studies with a high risk of bias did not alter the overall conclusions. The evidence was limited by imprecision, inconsistency, and indirectness in some cases. Most studies were conducted in high-income or middle-income countries, with varying prevalence of malnutrition and anemia. In summary, feeding children aged 12–23 months with follow-on formula or fortified milk may improve nutrient status (e.g., vitamin D, iron, and zinc) and reduce the risk of anemia and iron deficiency anemia compared to animal milk. However, the evidence on growth outcomes, long-term food preferences, and other health outcomes remains limited. The review highlights the need for further research, particularly on plant-based and lower-fat milks, as well as the effects of milk consumption in vulnerable populations.
